title: Reactions & Mechanisms
description: Nucleophiles and electrophiles, SN1/SN2/E1/E2, carbocation rearrangements, alkene and alkyne additions, alcohols, oxidation and reduction, Grignards, carbonyl and enolate chemistry, aromatic substitution and Diels–Alder.

cards.title: In a polar organic mechanism, what do a nucleophile and an electrophile each do with electrons?
cards.body:
A nucleophile donates an electron pair; an electrophile accepts one.

Nucleophiles are electron-rich (lone pairs, π bonds, anions). Electrophiles are electron-poor (carbocations, polarized carbonyl carbons, alkyl halide carbons).

Key idea: nucleophiles attack electrophiles, and nucleophilicity is a rate (kinetic) property, whereas basicity is thermodynamic.
cards.searchQuery: nucleophile electrophile definition electron pair donor acceptor

cards.title: In curved-arrow mechanisms, where must every arrow start?
cards.body:
At a source of electrons: a lone pair or a bond.

The arrow ends where the electron pair goes: forming a new bond or becoming a lone pair. Arrows never start at an atom or a positive charge.

Watch out: arrows show electron movement, not atom movement; a double-barbed arrow moves two electrons.
cards.searchQuery: curved arrow mechanism rules start at lone pair or bond

cards.title: Which is the better leaving group: $\ce{HO-}$ or $\ce{H2O}$? (give the formula)
cards.body:
H2O

Good leaving groups are **weak bases**, the conjugate bases of strong acids. Water (conjugate acid $\ce{H3O+}$, pKa about −1.7) is a much weaker base than hydroxide.

Example: this is why alcohols must be protonated by acid before they undergo $\mathrm{S_N1}$, $\mathrm{S_N2}$ or E1 reactions.
cards.searchQuery: leaving group ability water versus hydroxide weak base

cards.title: Which halide is the best leaving group in substitution and elimination reactions?
cards.body:
iodide

Leaving-group ability follows $\ce{I-} > \ce{Br-} > \ce{Cl-} \gg \ce{F-}$, the order of increasing basicity. Iodide is large, polarizable and the weakest base of the group.

Watch out: the same ordering holds for the strength of the corresponding hydrogen halide acids (HI strongest).
cards.searchQuery: best halide leaving group iodide trend

cards.title: Which reagent (abbreviation) converts an alcohol $\ce{ROH}$ into a tosylate $\ce{ROTs}$, turning OH into a good leaving group?
cards.body:
TsCl

Tosyl chloride with pyridine gives $\ce{ROTs}$. The C–O bond is not broken, so the stereocenter keeps its configuration.

Example: a later $\mathrm{S_N2}$ on the tosylate inverts the center, giving net inversion from the alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: tosyl chloride alcohol to tosylate leaving group retention

cards.title: In a polar protic solvent such as methanol, which is the better nucleophile: $\ce{I-}$ or $\ce{F-}$?
cards.body:
iodide

In protic solvents, small anions like fluoride are strongly **hydrogen bonded** and blunted, while large, polarizable iodide is less solvated and more nucleophilic.

Watch out: in polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF) this order reverses, because fluoride is then unsolvated.
cards.searchQuery: nucleophilicity trend halides polar protic solvent iodide fluoride

cards.title: Is neopentyl bromide, $\ce{(CH3)3CCH2Br}$, reactive in $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reactions? (yes or no)
cards.body:
no

It is a primary halide, but the bulky tert-butyl group on the adjacent (β) carbon **blocks backside attack**. It is about 100,000 times slower than ethyl bromide.

Watch out: the carbon bearing the leaving group is not the only one that matters; β-branching also slows $\mathrm{S_N2}$.
cards.searchQuery: neopentyl bromide SN2 unreactive steric hindrance beta branching

cards.title: What is the rate law of an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ reaction? (write in terms of RX)
cards.body:
rate = k[RX]

It is **first order** and independent of the nucleophile concentration, because the rate-determining step is ionization of the substrate.

Example: doubling the nucleophile concentration does not change the rate; doubling [RX] doubles it.
cards.searchQuery: SN1 rate law first order unimolecular k[RX]

cards.title: What is the rate-determining step of an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ reaction?
cards.body:
Ionization of the substrate to form the carbocation.

The C–X bond breaks heterolytically to give $\ce{R+}$ and $\ce{X-}$. Nucleophile capture is fast and not rate-limiting.

Why: anything that stabilizes the carbocation (tertiary, allylic, benzylic, polar protic solvent) speeds the reaction.
cards.searchQuery: SN1 rate determining step carbocation formation ionization

cards.title: Rank carbocations from most to least stable and give the main reason.
cards.body:
3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, because of alkyl **hyperconjugation** and induction.

Neighboring C–H and C–C σ bonds donate electron density into the empty p orbital. Allylic and benzylic cations are extra stable from resonance.

Example: the allyl cation is about as stable as a secondary alkyl cation; the benzyl cation resembles a secondary-to-tertiary one.
cards.searchQuery: carbocation stability order hyperconjugation tertiary secondary primary

cards.title: A secondary carbocation sits next to a quaternary carbon, as in $\ce{(CH3)3C-CH+-CH3}$. What type of rearrangement gives a tertiary cation?
cards.body:
1,2-methyl shift

A methyl group migrates with its bonding pair to the cationic carbon, so the positive charge moves to the former quaternary carbon, forming the tertiary cation $\ce{(CH3)2C+-CH(CH3)2}$.

Key idea: rearrangements are 1,2-shifts of H or alkyl that move the charge to a more stable position.
cards.searchQuery: carbocation rearrangement 1,2-methyl shift tertiary

cards.title: $\ce{HCl}$ adds to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene. What is the major product (IUPAC name)?
cards.body:
2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane

Protonation gives the secondary cation $\ce{(CH3)3C-CH+-CH3}$, which undergoes a **methyl shift** to the tertiary cation $\ce{(CH3)2C+-CH(CH3)2}$. Chloride then adds to that carbon.

Watch out: the unrearranged product, 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylbutane, is only minor.
cards.searchQuery: HCl 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene methyl shift product

cards.title: When a tertiary alkyl halide is solvolyzed in ethanol, does raising the temperature favor $\mathrm{S_N1}$ or E1?
cards.body:
E1

Elimination produces more molecules (an extra species is formed), so it has a more **positive entropy** and a higher activation energy; raising the temperature favors it.

Tip: heat favors elimination over substitution in general.
cards.searchQuery: temperature favors elimination over substitution E1 SN1

cards.title: What is the rate law of an E2 reaction of an alkyl halide RX with a base B? (as typed)
cards.body:
rate = k[RX][B]

E2 is **bimolecular**: the base removes the β-hydrogen as the leaving group departs in a single concerted step, so both species appear in the rate-determining step.

Example: doubling either [RX] or [base] doubles the rate.
cards.searchQuery: E2 rate law second order bimolecular alkyl halide base

cards.title: A tertiary alkyl halide reacts with $\ce{NaOEt}$ in ethanol. Which mechanism dominates?
cards.body:
E2

Tertiary halides are too hindered for $\mathrm{S_N2}$, and a **strong base** such as ethoxide forces bimolecular elimination rather than slow $\mathrm{S_N1}$/E1 ionization.

Tip: tertiary + strong base = E2; tertiary + weak base/nucleophile = $\mathrm{S_N1}$/E1.
cards.searchQuery: tertiary alkyl halide strong base E2 elimination NaOEt

cards.title: A primary alkyl halide (unhindered) reacts with $\ce{NaOCH3}$ in $\ce{CH3OH}$. Which mechanism dominates?
cards.body:
SN2

A primary substrate is easily approached from the back, and methoxide is a strong nucleophile that is not especially bulky, so substitution wins over elimination.

Watch out: a bulky base such as tert-butoxide flips the outcome toward E2, even for primary halides.
cards.searchQuery: primary alkyl halide sodium methoxide SN2 substitution

cards.title: 1-Bromobutane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol. What is the major mechanism?
cards.body:
E2

The tert-butoxide ion is bulky and a poor nucleophile, so it removes a β-hydrogen instead of attacking carbon. The major product is 1-butene.

Tip: bulky strong bases (tBuOK, LDA) favor E2 and the less-substituted (Hofmann) alkene.
cards.searchQuery: potassium tert-butoxide primary alkyl halide E2 bulky base

cards.title: To make tert-butyl methyl ether by a Williamson synthesis with $\ce{(CH3)3CO-K+}$, which alkyl halide should you use (give the formula)?
cards.body:
CH3I

The Williamson synthesis is an $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction, so the alkyl halide must be **methyl or primary**. Using $\ce{(CH3)3CCl}$ with methoxide would give mainly E2 elimination to isobutylene.

Key idea: put the hindered group on the alkoxide, not on the alkyl halide.
cards.searchQuery: Williamson ether synthesis tert-butyl methyl ether methyl iodide

cards.title: (R)-2-Bromobutane reacts with $\ce{NaCN}$ by $\mathrm{S_N2}$. What is the configuration (R or S) of the 2-cyanobutane formed?
cards.body:
S

The $\mathrm{S_N2}$ pathway inverts the stereocenter. In both compounds the priority order is leaving group or CN > ethyl > methyl > H, so inversion of geometry changes the label from R to S.

Watch out: inversion of geometry only changes R/S if the priorities keep the same order, so check the CIP ranking.
cards.searchQuery: SN2 inversion (R)-2-bromobutane cyanide product configuration

cards.title: Ethyl bromide reacts with sodium azide ($\ce{NaN3}$) in DMF. What is the organic product (formula)?
cards.body:
CH3CH2N3

Azide is an excellent nucleophile for $\mathrm{S_N2}$ in a polar aprotic solvent. The product, ethyl azide, can be reduced by $\ce{LiAlH4}$ or $\ce{H2}$/Pd to a primary amine.

Tip: azide then reduction is a clean way to make primary amines without over-alkylation.
cards.searchQuery: alkyl halide sodium azide SN2 alkyl azide amine synthesis

cards.title: Propene reacts with $\ce{HBr}$ in the presence of peroxides ($\ce{ROOR}$). What is the major product?
cards.body:
1-bromopropane

Peroxides initiate a **radical chain** mechanism. $\ce{Br\cdot}$ adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary radical, then abstracts H from HBr.

Watch out: this anti-Markovnikov result works for HBr only, not HCl or HI.
cards.searchQuery: anti-Markovnikov HBr peroxides propene 1-bromopropane radical

cards.title: What type of mechanism explains the anti-Markovnikov addition of $\ce{HBr}$ to an alkene in the presence of peroxides?
cards.body:
radical chain

The steps are initiation (peroxide cleaves to $\ce{RO\cdot}$, which makes $\ce{Br\cdot}$), then two propagation steps: $\ce{Br\cdot}$ adds to the alkene, and the carbon radical abstracts H from HBr.

Key idea: the more stable carbon radical forms, which puts Br on the less substituted carbon.
cards.searchQuery: radical chain mechanism HBr peroxide effect anti-Markovnikov

cards.title: 2-Methylpropene is treated with dilute aqueous $\ce{H2SO4}$. What is the major product?
cards.body:
2-Methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol)

Protonation gives the **tertiary carbocation**, water attacks it, and loss of $\ce{H+}$ gives the alcohol, with OH on the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov).

Watch out: the reaction is reversible; concentrated acid and heat drive the reverse dehydration back to the alkene.
cards.searchQuery: acid catalyzed hydration of 2-methylpropene tert-butyl alcohol

cards.title: 3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene reacts with (1) $\ce{Hg(OAc)2}$, $\ce{H2O}$ and (2) $\ce{NaBH4}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol

Oxymercuration-demercuration gives **Markovnikov** hydration through a bridged mercurinium ion, so no free carbocation forms and there is no methyl shift.

Example: acid-catalyzed hydration of the same alkene would give the rearranged tertiary alcohol, 2,3-dimethyl-2-butanol.
cards.searchQuery: oxymercuration demercuration no rearrangement 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene

cards.title: Is the addition of $\ce{BH3}$ across an alkene syn or anti?
cards.body:
syn

Boron and hydrogen add to the **same face** of the double bond in one concerted step. Oxidation with $\ce{H2O2}$/$\ce{NaOH}$ then replaces B with OH with retention.

Example: hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene gives trans-2-methylcyclohexanol, because H and OH add syn.
cards.searchQuery: hydroboration syn addition concerted stereochemistry

cards.title: What key intermediate accounts for the anti addition of $\ce{Br2}$ to an alkene?
cards.body:
bromonium ion

The alkene attacks $\ce{Br2}$ to form a three-membered cyclic **bromonium ion**. Bromide must attack from the opposite face, giving the anti (trans) product.

Example: cyclohexene plus $\ce{Br2}$ gives racemic trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
cards.searchQuery: bromonium ion intermediate anti addition bromine alkene

cards.title: Propene reacts with $\ce{Br2}$ in water. What is the major product (IUPAC name)?
cards.body:
1-bromo-2-propanol

Water is the solvent, so it attacks the bromonium ion at the more substituted carbon, which carries more positive charge. That puts OH on C2 and Br on C1.

Watch out: this is **Markovnikov** in the sense that OH (the nucleophile) goes to the more substituted carbon.
cards.searchQuery: halohydrin formation propene bromine water regiochemistry

cards.title: 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene is hydrogenated with $\ce{H2}$ over Pd/C. Is the product cis- or trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane?
cards.body:
cis

Both hydrogens add from the face of the alkene bound to the metal surface, so the addition is **syn**. The two methyl groups end up on the same side.

Tip: catalytic hydrogenation is syn; dissolving-metal reduction of alkynes is anti.
cards.searchQuery: catalytic hydrogenation syn addition cis product dimethylcyclohexene

cards.title: What common peroxy acid (abbreviation) converts an alkene into an epoxide?
cards.body:
mCPBA

**meta-Chloroperoxybenzoic acid** transfers an oxygen to the alkene in one concerted step (butterfly mechanism). The reaction is a stereospecific syn addition: a cis alkene gives a cis-substituted epoxide.

Example: cyclohexene plus mCPBA gives cyclohexene oxide (7-oxabicyclo[4.1.0]heptane).
cards.searchQuery: mCPBA epoxidation alkene meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid

cards.title: Cyclohexene oxide is treated with aqueous $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product (IUPAC name, with stereo descriptor)?
cards.body:
trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol

Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the back side, opening it with inversion at that carbon. The OH groups end up **anti**, so the diol is trans (formed as a racemate).

Watch out: OsO4 gives the cis diol, so epoxidation plus hydrolysis and OsO4 are complementary.
cards.searchQuery: epoxide acid hydrolysis trans diol cyclohexene oxide anti

cards.title: Cyclohexene reacts with $\ce{OsO4}$ followed by $\ce{NaHSO3}$ (or with cold, dilute $\ce{KMnO4}$, $\ce{NaOH}$). What is the product?
cards.body:
cis-1,2-cyclohexanediol

The reagent adds both oxygens to the **same face** through a cyclic osmate ester, which is a syn dihydroxylation. The product is the meso (cis) diol.

Why it matters: OsO4 is toxic and costly, so it is often used catalytically with NMO.
cards.searchQuery: OsO4 syn dihydroxylation cyclohexene cis diol

cards.title: Cyclohexene is treated with (1) $\ce{O3}$ and (2) $\ce{(CH3)2S}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
hexanedial

Ozonolysis **cleaves the C=C bond** and gives a carbonyl at each carbon. In a ring, both ends stay in the same molecule, giving a dialdehyde, $\ce{OHC(CH2)4CHO}$.

Watch out: an oxidative workup ($\ce{H2O2}$) would turn the aldehydes into carboxylic acids, giving hexanedioic (adipic) acid.
cards.searchQuery: ozonolysis cyclohexene hexanedial dimethyl sulfide workup

cards.title: How does the heat of hydrogenation of an alkene relate to its stability?
cards.body:
The more stable the alkene, the less heat it releases.

All alkenes with the same carbon skeleton give the same alkane, so differences in heat released reflect differences in the alkene's starting energy.

Example: trans-2-butene releases about 27.6 kcal/mol and cis-2-butene about 28.6 kcal/mol, so trans is more stable by about 1 kcal/mol.
cards.searchQuery: heat of hydrogenation alkene stability trans cis comparison

cards.title: Which 2-butene isomer is more stable: cis or trans?
cards.body:
trans

In the cis isomer the two methyl groups are on the same side and suffer **steric strain**. The trans isomer avoids it and is more stable by about 1 kcal/mol.

Tip: more substituted alkenes and trans alkenes are generally more stable.
cards.searchQuery: trans-2-butene more stable than cis steric strain

cards.title: Which named reaction converts an alkene to a cyclopropane using $\ce{CH2I2}$ and a zinc-copper couple?
cards.body:
Simmons-Smith

The zinc carbenoid ($\ce{ICH2ZnI}$) transfers a $\ce{CH2}$ group in one concerted step. It is **stereospecific**: a cis alkene gives a cis-disubstituted cyclopropane.

Watch out: no free carbene forms, so there is no rearrangement and no insertion.
cards.searchQuery: Simmons-Smith cyclopropanation CH2I2 Zn(Cu) alkene

cards.title: Why do hydroboration-oxidation and oxymercuration avoid carbocation rearrangements, unlike acid-catalyzed hydration?
cards.body:
Neither passes through a free carbocation.

Hydroboration is a concerted four-center addition, and oxymercuration uses a bridged **mercurinium ion** that holds the positive charge. Without a discrete cation there is no 1,2-shift.

Key idea: use these methods when a rearrangement-prone alkene must give a clean alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: why no carbocation rearrangement hydroboration oxymercuration

cards.title: Propyne reacts with 2 equivalents of $\ce{HBr}$ (no peroxides). What is the product?
cards.body:
2,2-dibromopropane

The first addition follows Markovnikov's rule to give 2-bromopropene, and the second puts the second Br on the same carbon, giving a **geminal** dibromide.

Why: bromine stabilizes the adjacent carbocation by lone-pair donation.
cards.searchQuery: propyne two equivalents HBr geminal dibromide 2,2-dibromopropane

cards.title: 1-Butyne is treated with $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{H2SO4}$ and $\ce{HgSO4}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-butanone

Markovnikov addition of water gives an enol, which **tautomerizes** to the more stable ketone. A terminal alkyne therefore gives a methyl ketone.

Watch out: hydration of an alkyne gives a carbonyl compound, not an alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: alkyne hydration HgSO4 methyl ketone 1-butyne 2-butanone

cards.title: 1-Butyne reacts with (1) disiamylborane (or 9-BBN) and (2) $\ce{H2O2}$, $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
butanal

Hydroboration puts boron on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov); oxidation gives an enol that tautomerizes to the **aldehyde**.

Tip: use a bulky borane so that only one B–H adds to the alkyne rather than two.
cards.searchQuery: alkyne hydroboration oxidation terminal alkyne aldehyde butanal

cards.title: 2-Butyne is treated with $\ce{Na}$ in liquid $\ce{NH3}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
trans-2-butene

A dissolving-metal reduction proceeds through a radical anion and a vinyl radical, giving the more stable **trans** (anti addition) alkene.

Watch out: terminal alkynes are not reduced this way; they are deprotonated instead.
cards.searchQuery: Na NH3 alkyne reduction trans alkene dissolving metal

cards.title: 2-Butyne is treated with $\ce{H2}$ and Lindlar's catalyst. What is the product?
cards.body:
cis-2-butene

The poisoned palladium catalyst delivers both hydrogens to the same face (**syn addition**) and stops at the alkene stage.

Tip: Lindlar (or P-2 nickel) gives cis alkenes; Na/NH3 gives trans alkenes.
cards.searchQuery: Lindlar catalyst alkyne to cis alkene syn hydrogenation

cards.title: Propyne is treated with (1) $\ce{NaNH2}$ and (2) $\ce{CH3CH2Br}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-pentyne

The acetylide anion is a strong nucleophile that displaces bromide in an $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction, forming a new C–C bond: $\ce{CH3C#C-CH2CH3}$.

Example: this builds longer alkynes from terminal ones.
cards.searchQuery: acetylide alkylation SN2 propyne ethyl bromide 2-pentyne

cards.title: Why does an acetylide ion give poor yields when treated with a secondary or tertiary alkyl halide?
cards.body:
It acts as a base and causes E2 elimination.

The acetylide is a strong base and the hindered electrophile resists $\mathrm{S_N2}$ backside attack, so elimination wins.

Tip: acetylide alkylation works with methyl and primary halides only.
cards.searchQuery: acetylide secondary alkyl halide E2 elimination alkylation limitation

cards.title: What is the mechanism for acid-catalyzed dehydration of a tertiary alcohol?
cards.body:
E1

Protonation of the OH gives water as a leaving group, which departs to give a carbocation. A base (water) then removes a β-proton to form the alkene.

Tip: the order of ease is 3° > 2° > 1°, matching carbocation stability.
cards.searchQuery: acid catalyzed dehydration tertiary alcohol E1 mechanism

cards.title: 3-Methyl-2-butanol is heated with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$. What is the major alkene (IUPAC name)?
cards.body:
2-methyl-2-butene

Loss of water gives a secondary cation, which undergoes a **hydride shift** from C3 to give a tertiary cation. Loss of H⁺ then forms the most substituted (Zaitsev) alkene.

Watch out: dehydration passes through cations, so always check for 1,2-shifts.
cards.searchQuery: dehydration 3-methyl-2-butanol hydride shift 2-methyl-2-butene

cards.title: Which reagent (formula), used with pyridine, dehydrates an alcohol by an E2 pathway and avoids carbocation rearrangements?
cards.body:
POCl3

The OH reacts with $\ce{POCl3}$ to form a dichlorophosphate, a good leaving group. Pyridine then acts as the base for **E2** elimination.

Why it matters: no carbocation forms, so there is no rearrangement and the conditions are milder than hot acid.
cards.searchQuery: POCl3 pyridine alcohol dehydration E2 no rearrangement

cards.title: Which reagent (formula) converts a primary alcohol into an alkyl chloride, giving only gaseous byproducts?
cards.body:
SOCl2

Thionyl chloride gives $\ce{R-Cl}$ plus $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{HCl}$, both gases that leave the mixture. With pyridine the chloride attacks by $\mathrm{S_N2}$, giving **inversion** at a stereocenter.

Tip: it also converts carboxylic acids to acid chlorides.
cards.searchQuery: thionyl chloride SOCl2 alcohol to alkyl chloride SN2

cards.title: Which reagent (formula) converts a secondary alcohol into an alkyl bromide with inversion and no rearrangement?
cards.body:
PBr3

The alcohol oxygen attacks phosphorus, creating a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it by $\mathrm{S_N2}$.

Watch out: since it is $\mathrm{S_N2}$, it works best on primary and secondary alcohols, not tertiary ones.
cards.searchQuery: PBr3 alcohol to alkyl bromide SN2 inversion

cards.title: In the Lucas test ($\ce{ZnCl2}$ in conc. $\ce{HCl}$), which class of alcohol reacts immediately, giving cloudiness?
cards.body:
tertiary

The reagent converts alcohols to alkyl chlorides by an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ pathway, so 3° alcohols react at once, 2° in a few minutes, and 1° essentially not at room temperature.

Key idea: reactivity tracks carbocation stability.
cards.searchQuery: Lucas test tertiary alcohol ZnCl2 HCl SN1 reactivity

cards.title: 1-Propanol is treated with PCC in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
propanal

PCC is a mild chromium(VI) oxidant used in the **absence of water**, so the reaction stops at the aldehyde.

Watch out: with aqueous oxidants like Jones reagent, the aldehyde hydrate forms and is oxidized further to the acid.
cards.searchQuery: PCC oxidation primary alcohol aldehyde propanal

cards.title: 1-Butanol is treated with $\ce{CrO3}$, $\ce{H2SO4}$ and acetone (Jones reagent). What is the product?
cards.body:
butanoic acid

Jones reagent is a strong aqueous chromic acid oxidant. A primary alcohol goes through the aldehyde and its hydrate and ends at the **carboxylic acid**.

Example: a secondary alcohol stops at the ketone; a tertiary alcohol does not react.
cards.searchQuery: Jones oxidation primary alcohol carboxylic acid butanoic acid

cards.title: Cyclohexanol is oxidized with $\ce{Na2Cr2O7}$/$\ce{H2SO4}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
cyclohexanone

A secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, which has no H on the carbonyl carbon and resists further oxidation.

Tip: oxidation removes the carbinol H and the O–H hydrogen; this is the basis of the colour change from orange Cr(VI) to green Cr(III).
cards.searchQuery: oxidation of secondary alcohol cyclohexanol cyclohexanone dichromate

cards.title: Why can't a tertiary alcohol be oxidized by chromic acid or PCC?
cards.body:
It has no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon.

Oxidation requires removing the C–H as the C=O forms, and without that hydrogen the reaction cannot proceed without breaking C–C bonds.

Key idea: primary and secondary alcohols oxidize; tertiary alcohols do not.
cards.searchQuery: tertiary alcohol cannot oxidize no hydrogen carbinol carbon

cards.title: Which named oxidation uses DMSO, oxalyl chloride and triethylamine to convert alcohols to aldehydes or ketones?
cards.body:
Swern oxidation

It is a mild, metal-free oxidation run at low temperature (about −78 °C). Primary alcohols stop at the **aldehyde**, and secondary alcohols give ketones.

Watch out: it releases dimethyl sulfide, which smells foul, plus CO and $\ce{CO2}$.
cards.searchQuery: Swern oxidation DMSO oxalyl chloride triethylamine

cards.title: 2-Pentanone is treated with $\ce{NaBH4}$ in methanol, then workup. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-pentanol

Borohydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon. The oxygen is protonated by the solvent, giving a **secondary alcohol**.

Watch out: the product is racemic, since hydride can attack either face of the planar ketone.
cards.searchQuery: NaBH4 reduction ketone secondary alcohol 2-pentanone

cards.title: Ethyl acetate is treated with (1) $\ce{LiAlH4}$ and (2) $\ce{H3O+}$. What alcohol(s) result?
cards.body:
ethanol

Two equivalents form: $\ce{LiAlH4}$ reduces the acyl part to a primary alcohol, and the alkoxy part is released as an alcohol. Here both parts are ethanol.

Key idea: $\ce{NaBH4}$ is too weak to reduce esters, but $\ce{LiAlH4}$ is not.
cards.searchQuery: LiAlH4 reduces ester ethyl acetate two ethanol

cards.title: Butanoic acid is treated with (1) $\ce{LiAlH4}$ and (2) $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
1-butanol

$\ce{LiAlH4}$ reduces carboxylic acids all the way to **primary alcohols**; the aldehyde intermediate is more reactive than the acid, so it cannot be isolated.

Watch out: $\ce{NaBH4}$ does not reduce carboxylic acids.
cards.searchQuery: LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acid primary alcohol butanoic acid

cards.title: Propylene oxide (methyloxirane) reacts with $\ce{NaOCH3}$ in $\ce{CH3OH}$. What is the major product?
cards.body:
1-methoxy-2-propanol

Under basic or nucleophilic conditions, the nucleophile attacks the **less hindered carbon** by $\mathrm{S_N2}$, so methoxide ends up on the terminal $\ce{CH2}$.

Watch out: under acidic conditions, attack shifts toward the more substituted carbon.
cards.searchQuery: epoxide ring opening basic conditions less hindered carbon propylene oxide

cards.title: Anisole ($\ce{C6H5OCH3}$) is heated with excess $\ce{HBr}$. Which organic compounds form?
cards.body:
phenol and bromomethane

Protonated ether is cleaved by bromide attacking the **methyl** carbon by $\mathrm{S_N2}$. Bromide cannot attack the sp2 aryl carbon, so no bromobenzene forms.

Tip: aryl alkyl ethers always cleave to a phenol plus an alkyl halide.
cards.searchQuery: anisole cleavage HBr phenol methyl bromide ether cleavage

cards.title: What organic product forms when $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ is exposed to water?
cards.body:
methane

A Grignard reagent is a strong base (the conjugate acid of a carbanion has pKa about 50), so water protonates it instantly: $\ce{CH3MgBr + H2O -> CH4 + Mg(OH)Br}$.

Why: this is why Grignard reactions need **dry ether** and no OH, NH or acidic C–H groups on the substrate.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard reagent reacts with water methane strong base anhydrous

cards.title: Phenylmagnesium bromide is treated with (1) $\ce{CO2}$ and (2) $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
benzoic acid

The Grignard carbon attacks $\ce{CO2}$ to give a carboxylate, which acid protonates. The product has **one more carbon** than the Grignard's alkyl group.

Tip: Grignard plus $\ce{CO2}$ is a standard way to build a carboxylic acid from a halide.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard carbon dioxide carboxylic acid benzoic acid synthesis

cards.title: $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ reacts with formaldehyde, $\ce{H2C=O}$, and then aqueous acid. What is the product?
cards.body:
ethanol

Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl carbon. Formaldehyde always gives a **primary alcohol** with one more carbon than the Grignard's R group.

Key idea: formaldehyde gives 1° alcohols, other aldehydes give 2° alcohols, ketones give 3° alcohols.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard formaldehyde primary alcohol methylmagnesium bromide

cards.title: $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ reacts with acetaldehyde, then $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-propanol

The methyl adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving an alkoxide that is protonated on workup. The product has two carbons on the carbinol carbon, so it is a **secondary alcohol**.

Example: using ethylmagnesium bromide and formaldehyde would give 1-propanol instead.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard aldehyde secondary alcohol methylmagnesium bromide acetaldehyde

cards.title: $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ reacts with acetone, then $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-methyl-2-propanol

A ketone gives a **tertiary alcohol**. Here the carbinol carbon bears three methyl groups, giving tert-butyl alcohol.

Watch out: a Grignard reagent adds only once to an aldehyde or ketone, so the alcohol is the final product.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard ketone tertiary alcohol acetone methylmagnesium bromide

cards.title: Methyl benzoate reacts with excess $\ce{CH3MgBr}$, then $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-phenyl-2-propanol

The first equivalent adds, then expels methoxide to give a ketone (acetophenone). The ketone is **more reactive** than the ester, so a second equivalent adds immediately.

Watch out: esters give tertiary alcohols with two identical new R groups; you cannot stop at the ketone.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard ester two equivalents tertiary alcohol methyl benzoate

cards.title: $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$ reacts with ethylene oxide, then $\ce{H3O+}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
1-butanol

The Grignard attacks the epoxide's less hindered carbon, opening the ring. The product is a primary alcohol with **two more carbons**: $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2OH}$.

Tip: ethylene oxide plus RMgX lengthens a chain by two carbons.
cards.searchQuery: Grignard ethylene oxide primary alcohol two carbon extension

cards.title: Why is the carbon of a C=O group electrophilic?
cards.body:
Oxygen is more electronegative, so the C=O bond is polarized toward O.

The resonance form $\ce{C+-O-}$ places partial positive charge on carbon, and nucleophiles attack there, pushing the π electrons onto oxygen.

Key idea: nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl converts sp2 carbon to sp3 (a tetrahedral intermediate).
cards.searchQuery: carbonyl carbon electrophilic polarization nucleophilic addition

cards.title: Toward nucleophilic addition, which is more reactive: acetaldehyde or acetone?
cards.body:
acetaldehyde

Two effects: the aldehyde has less **steric hindrance** (one H instead of an alkyl group), and the second alkyl group in a ketone donates electron density that stabilizes the carbonyl.

Example: formaldehyde is more reactive still.
cards.searchQuery: aldehydes more reactive than ketones nucleophilic addition steric electronic

cards.title: A ketone reacts with ethylene glycol and an acid catalyst (with water removed). What functional group forms?
cards.body:
acetal

A cyclic acetal (technically a ketal) forms. It is stable to bases, Grignard reagents, hydrides and nucleophiles, and is removed by **aqueous acid**.

Tip: use it to protect a ketone while reacting an ester elsewhere in the molecule with $\ce{LiAlH4}$.
cards.searchQuery: acetal protecting group ketone ethylene glycol acid catalyst

cards.title: Why is imine formation from a ketone and a primary amine fastest near pH 4-5?
cards.body:
Acid must protonate the carbinolamine OH, but too much acid protonates the amine.

At low pH the amine becomes $\ce{RNH3+}$ and is no longer nucleophilic. At high pH there is too little acid to turn OH into a leaving group (water).

Key idea: the rate peaks where enough free amine and enough protonated intermediate coexist.
cards.searchQuery: imine formation pH 4-5 optimum carbinolamine mechanism

cards.title: A ketone reacts with a secondary amine such as pyrrolidine under acid catalysis. What functional group forms?
cards.body:
enamine

With no N–H left on the iminium ion, loss of an **α-proton** gives a C=C–N unit instead of an imine.

Why it matters: enamines are enol-like nucleophiles used in the Stork enamine alkylation.
cards.searchQuery: enamine formation secondary amine ketone pyrrolidine

cards.title: Cyclohexanone reacts with $\ce{Ph3P=CH2}$. What is the organic product?
cards.body:
methylenecyclohexane

The Wittig reaction swaps the C=O for a C=C: the carbonyl oxygen leaves as **triphenylphosphine oxide**, whose strong P=O bond drives the reaction.

Example: it places the double bond exactly where the C=O was, unlike elimination routes.
cards.searchQuery: Wittig reaction cyclohexanone methylenecyclohexane phosphorus ylide

cards.title: What functional-group product forms when an aldehyde or ketone adds $\ce{HCN}$ (from $\ce{KCN}$/$\ce{H+}$)?
cards.body:
cyanohydrin

Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated, giving a carbon bearing both OH and $\ce{C#N}$. The new product has **one more carbon**.

Example: acetone gives acetone cyanohydrin, $\ce{(CH3)2C(OH)CN}$.
cards.searchQuery: cyanohydrin formation HCN aldehyde ketone nucleophilic addition

cards.title: What is the approximate pKa of an α-hydrogen of a simple ketone such as acetone?
cards.body:
19

The enolate conjugate base is stabilized by resonance onto oxygen. Acetone's pKa is about 19-20, many units more acidic than an alkane's.

Example: ester α-H are less acidic (about 25) and 1,3-diketones are about 9.
cards.searchQuery: alpha hydrogen pKa ketone 19 enolate acidity

cards.title: Which strong, bulky base (abbreviation) at −78 °C converts an unsymmetrical ketone mainly into its kinetic enolate?
cards.body:
LDA

Lithium diisopropylamide removes the more accessible, **less substituted** α-proton quickly and irreversibly.

Key idea: LDA at low temperature gives the kinetic (less substituted) enolate; weaker alkoxide bases in equilibrium give the thermodynamic (more substituted) one.
cards.searchQuery: LDA kinetic enolate less substituted unsymmetrical ketone low temperature

cards.title: Acetaldehyde is treated with dilute $\ce{NaOH}$ at low temperature. What is the aldol addition product?
cards.body:
3-hydroxybutanal

The enolate of one molecule adds to the carbonyl of a second: $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$, a **β-hydroxy aldehyde**.

Tip: aldol means aldehyde + alcohol; the new C–C bond is between the α-carbon and the carbonyl carbon.
cards.searchQuery: aldol addition acetaldehyde 3-hydroxybutanal base

cards.title: Heating the aldol product of acetaldehyde with base causes dehydration. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-butenal

The β-hydroxy aldehyde loses water through an E1cB pathway to give an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde, $\ce{CH3CH=CHCHO}$ (crotonaldehyde). The **conjugation** drives the dehydration.

Watch out: the product has a C=C conjugated with C=O, which is why heating favors condensation.
cards.searchQuery: aldol condensation dehydration crotonaldehyde 2-butenal E1cB

cards.title: Cyclohexanone is treated with (1) LDA and (2) $\ce{CH3I}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
2-methylcyclohexanone

The enolate attacks methyl iodide by $\mathrm{S_N2}$ at its α-carbon, forming a new C–C bond.

Watch out: use methyl, primary or benzylic/allylic halides; secondary and tertiary halides undergo E2 with the enolate.
cards.searchQuery: enolate alkylation LDA methyl iodide 2-methylcyclohexanone SN2

cards.title: Ethyl acetate is treated with $\ce{NaOEt}$ in ethanol, then acid. What is the Claisen condensation product?
cards.body:
ethyl 3-oxobutanoate

The ester enolate attacks a second ester and ethoxide is lost, giving $\ce{CH3COCH2CO2Et}$ (ethyl acetoacetate), a **β-keto ester**.

Why: the final deprotonation of the very acidic β-keto ester (pKa about 11) drives the equilibrium, so a full equivalent of base is needed.
cards.searchQuery: Claisen condensation ethyl acetate ethyl acetoacetate beta-keto ester

cards.title: Which reagent (formula) selectively reduces an iminium ion in the presence of the starting ketone during reductive amination?
cards.body:
NaBH3CN

Sodium cyanoborohydride is a **milder** hydride donor than $\ce{NaBH4}$ at pH 6-7, so it reduces the protonated imine but not the ketone.

Example: cyclohexanone, $\ce{CH3NH2}$ and $\ce{NaBH3CN}$ give N-methylcyclohexylamine in one pot.
cards.searchQuery: reductive amination sodium cyanoborohydride iminium selective

cards.title: Which named reaction reduces a ketone C=O to $\ce{CH2}$ using $\ce{H2NNH2}$ and $\ce{KOH}$ with heat?
cards.body:
Wolff-Kishner

The ketone forms a hydrazone, which loses $\ce{N2}$ under strong base to give the alkane.

Tip: Wolff-Kishner is basic, whereas **Clemmensen** ($\ce{Zn(Hg)}$, $\ce{HCl}$) is acidic; choose by what else the molecule tolerates.
cards.searchQuery: Wolff-Kishner reduction hydrazine KOH ketone to alkane

cards.title: Diethyl malonate is treated with $\ce{NaOEt}$, then $\ce{CH3CH2Br}$, then $\ce{H3O+}$ and heat. What is the final carboxylic acid?
cards.body:
butanoic acid

The malonate enolate is alkylated, then hydrolysis gives a diacid that **decarboxylates** on heating, leaving $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COOH}$.

Key idea: the malonic ester synthesis makes substituted acetic acids, here $\ce{CH3CH2-CH2COOH}$.
cards.searchQuery: malonic ester synthesis alkylation decarboxylation butanoic acid

cards.title: Which organometallic reagent type adds 1,4 (conjugate addition) to an α,β-unsaturated ketone, e.g. $\ce{(CH3)2CuLi}$?
cards.body:
Gilman reagent

Lithium dialkylcuprates are **soft nucleophiles** and deliver R to the β-carbon of an enone. Grignard and organolithium reagents usually add 1,2 to the carbonyl instead.

Example: $\ce{(CH3)2CuLi}$ plus cyclohexenone gives 3-methylcyclohexanone after workup.
cards.searchQuery: Gilman reagent conjugate addition enone cuprate 1,4

cards.title: Acetic acid is heated with ethanol and a catalytic amount of $\ce{H2SO4}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
ethyl acetate

Fischer esterification is an **equilibrium**. It is pushed toward the ester by using excess alcohol or by removing water.

Watch out: the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, which activates the acid toward attack by the alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: Fischer esterification acetic acid ethanol ethyl acetate equilibrium

cards.title: Acetyl chloride reacts with excess $\ce{NH3}$. What is the organic product?
cards.body:
acetamide

Ammonia attacks the carbonyl by nucleophilic acyl substitution and chloride leaves. The second equivalent of $\ce{NH3}$ neutralizes the $\ce{HCl}$ formed, giving $\ce{NH4Cl}$.

Tip: acid chlorides react rapidly with water, alcohols and amines at room temperature.
cards.searchQuery: acid chloride ammonia amide nucleophilic acyl substitution acetamide

cards.title: Rank these carboxylic acid derivatives from most to least reactive toward nucleophiles: ester, acyl chloride, amide, anhydride.
cards.body:
Acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.

Reactivity tracks leaving-group ability and how little the substituent donates electrons into the C=O. Chloride is a great leaving group; the nitrogen of an amide donates strongly by **resonance**.

Key idea: a more reactive derivative can be converted into a less reactive one, but not the reverse (without activation).
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid derivatives reactivity order acyl chloride anhydride ester amide

cards.title: Ethyl acetate is heated with aqueous $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the organic product (before any acidification)?
cards.body:
sodium acetate

Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl, ethoxide leaves, and the acid formed is immediately deprotonated. This irreversible step makes **saponification** go to completion.

Watch out: acidic hydrolysis is an equilibrium; basic hydrolysis is irreversible.
cards.searchQuery: saponification ester hydrolysis base sodium acetate irreversible

cards.title: Propanenitrile is treated with (1) $\ce{LiAlH4}$ and (2) water. What is the product?
cards.body:
1-propanamine

$\ce{LiAlH4}$ adds two hydrides to the $\ce{C#N}$ carbon, giving a **primary amine** with the same number of carbons: $\ce{CH3CH2CH2NH2}$.

Example: acid hydrolysis of a nitrile instead gives the carboxylic acid.
cards.searchQuery: nitrile reduction LiAlH4 primary amine propanenitrile

cards.title: How many π electrons does the cyclopentadienyl anion have, making it aromatic by Hückel's rule?
cards.body:
6

The ring has two C=C bonds (4 π electrons) plus the carbanion's lone pair in a p orbital, totaling 6 = 4n + 2 with $n = 1$.

Why it matters: this explains why cyclopentadiene has an unusually low pKa of about 16 for a hydrocarbon.
cards.searchQuery: cyclopentadienyl anion aromatic Huckel rule 6 pi electrons

cards.title: What electrophile attacks benzene in nitration with $\ce{HNO3}$ and $\ce{H2SO4}$? (give the formula)
cards.body:
NO2+

Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to form the **nitronium ion**, $\ce{NO2+}$.

Tip: in electrophilic aromatic substitution the first step (electrophile attack, forming the arenium ion) is rate-determining.
cards.searchQuery: nitronium ion electrophile nitration benzene mechanism

cards.title: Benzene reacts with $\ce{Br2}$ and $\ce{FeBr3}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
bromobenzene

$\ce{FeBr3}$ polarizes $\ce{Br2}$ to give a strongly electrophilic Br. Attack gives the arenium ion, then loss of H⁺ **restores aromaticity**.

Watch out: benzene does not undergo addition with $\ce{Br2}$ alone, because that would destroy aromatic stabilization.
cards.searchQuery: bromination benzene FeBr3 electrophilic aromatic substitution bromobenzene

cards.title: Benzene reacts with 1-chloropropane and $\ce{AlCl3}$. What is the major product (IUPAC name)?
cards.body:
isopropylbenzene

The primary carbocation-like species undergoes a **hydride shift** to the secondary cation, which then alkylates the ring, giving cumene.

Tip: to get n-propylbenzene, acylate with propanoyl chloride and then reduce the C=O (Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner).
cards.searchQuery: Friedel-Crafts alkylation rearrangement 1-chloropropane cumene

cards.title: Benzene reacts with $\ce{CH3COCl}$ and $\ce{AlCl3}$. What is the product?
cards.body:
acetophenone

The electrophile is the **acylium ion**, $\ce{CH3C#O+}$, which does not rearrange. The ketone product deactivates the ring, so only one acyl group is added.

Example: unlike alkylation, acylation avoids rearrangement and polyalkylation.
cards.searchQuery: Friedel-Crafts acylation acetophenone acylium ion benzene

cards.title: Is a nitro group on a benzene ring an ortho/para or a meta director in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
cards.body:
meta

The nitro group withdraws electrons by resonance and induction, **deactivating** the ring. Ortho and para attack put positive charge next to the electron-poor nitrogen, so meta is the least bad.

Key idea: strongly deactivating groups (NO2, CN, C=O, SO3H) are meta directors.
cards.searchQuery: nitro group meta director deactivating electrophilic aromatic substitution

cards.title: Nitration of toluene gives mainly which ring positions relative to the methyl group?
cards.body:
ortho and para

The methyl group is **activating** (hyperconjugation and induction). Attack at ortho or para gives an arenium ion with a tertiary carbocation resonance form.

Watch out: a mixture forms, so toluene reacts faster than benzene and gives both o- and p-nitrotoluene.
cards.searchQuery: toluene nitration ortho para activating methyl group directing

cards.title: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with ethylene in a Diels-Alder reaction. What is the product?
cards.body:
cyclohexene

The diene (4 π electrons) and dienophile (2 π electrons) form two new σ bonds and one new π bond in a single concerted $[4+2]$ cycloaddition.

Watch out: the diene must be able to adopt the **s-cis** conformation to react.
cards.searchQuery: Diels-Alder butadiene ethylene cyclohexene [4+2] cycloaddition

cards.title: Cyclopentadiene reacts with maleic anhydride. Which stereochemical product (exo or endo) is favored kinetically?
cards.body:
endo

The anhydride carbonyls tuck beneath the developing π system, stabilized by **secondary orbital overlap**, so the endo adduct forms faster.

Example: the endo product is the kinetic one; the exo can be more stable thermodynamically.
cards.searchQuery: Diels-Alder endo rule cyclopentadiene maleic anhydride kinetic product

cards.title: In radical halogenation of alkanes, which halogen is more selective for the most substituted C–H: $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$?
cards.body:
Br2

The hydrogen abstraction by $\ce{Br\cdot}$ is endothermic with a late, product-like transition state, so it is highly sensitive to radical stability.

Example: bromination of propane gives about 97% 2-bromopropane, while chlorination gives roughly 55%.
cards.searchQuery: radical halogenation selectivity bromine versus chlorine Hammond postulate

cards.title: Cyclohexene is treated with NBS and light (or peroxide). What is the product?
cards.body:
3-bromocyclohexene

NBS supplies a **low, steady concentration** of $\ce{Br2}$, so allylic substitution by a radical chain beats addition across the double bond.

Why: the allylic C–H is weak (about 88 kcal/mol) because the allylic radical is resonance-stabilized.
cards.searchQuery: NBS allylic bromination cyclohexene 3-bromocyclohexene radical

cards.title: What is the name of the resonance-stabilized carbocation intermediate formed when an electrophile attacks benzene?
cards.body:
arenium ion

Also called the **sigma complex** or Wheland intermediate. The positive charge is delocalized over three ring carbons (ortho and para to the new bond), and the attacked carbon is sp3.

Key idea: loss of H⁺ from that sp3 carbon restores aromaticity; it is fast compared with the electrophile attack.
cards.searchQuery: arenium ion sigma complex electrophilic aromatic substitution intermediate
